nameStory: The horned bladderwort gets its name from the distinctive horn-like spur that projects from each bright yellow flower, looking like a tiny curved horn. The 'bladderwort' part comes from the microscopic bladder-like traps hidden on its roots that vacuum up tiny water creatures like aquatic mosquito larvae.
description: Horned bladderwort is a small carnivorous plant that produces cheerful yellow flowers on slender stalks rising 4-12 inches above wet ground or shallow water. Unlike the dramatic Venus flytraps you might know, this unassuming plant does its hunting underwater with tiny bladder traps you can't see without a magnifying glass. The flowers look like miniature snapdragons with a curved horn-like spur sticking out the back. Most of the plant stays hidden below the surface, making the bright yellow blooms seem to float mysteriously above the water.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers shaped like tiny snapdragons, each with a distinctive curved horn or spur projecting backward from the base - this spur is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Flowers appear to rise directly from water or wet soil on thin, leafless stalks 4-12 inches tall, with most of the plant hidden underwater or in saturated soil

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, thread-like underwater leaves that are often invisible from the surface - you might need to gently lift the plant to see the delicate, divided foliage below

idTips.label: Habitat Clues
idTips.description: Always found in or right at the edge of water - wet sandy shores, shallow pools, or saturated peaty soil that squelches underfoot

habitat: Look for horned bladderwort in shallow, acidic waters and constantly wet soils throughout New England - especially the edges of ponds, quiet stream backwaters, and boggy areas. It thrives in peaty or sandy soils that stay saturated year-round, often growing alongside sphagnum moss, sedges, and other bog plants. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, particularly in areas where the water level fluctuates seasonally.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin emerging from winter dormancy, with the first yellow flower spikes appearing in late spring as waters warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the distinctive horned yellow flowers are most abundant and easiest to spot rising above the water.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin to retreat underground, though some late blooms may persist into early fall in warmer areas.
seasonality.winter: Plants survive as small underground structures called turions, completely invisible above ground until spring returns.

funFact: Each horned bladderwort is a tiny underwater predator with hundreds of microscopic bladder traps that can suck in a water flea faster than you can blink - the traps create a vacuum so powerful they capture prey in less than a millisecond, making them among the fastest predators on Earth!
confusionNotes: The horn-like spur on each flower makes this species fairly distinctive among bladderworts, but other yellow-flowered bladderworts can look similar from a distance. Remember the horn rule: if you see a obvious curved spur projecting backward from bright yellow snapdragon-like flowers in wet areas, you've found horned bladderwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being carnivorous plants, bladderworts are not dangerous to humans at all - their tiny traps only catch microscopic water creatures. Many people are surprised to learn that New England has numerous native carnivorous plants, with bladderworts being among the most common but least noticed.
compareHints: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater. While common bladderwort floats freely in deeper water and purple bladderwort has pinkish flowers, horned bladderwort stays anchored in shallow, muddy areas with its distinctive golden horned blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth.
Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size.
